passages.passage_text:
Students of religion have long worked from an assumption so intuitive that it seldom receives defense: that ritual is the outward expression of inner belief. On this view, a community first holds convictions about the divine, the cosmos, or the afterlife, and then devises gestures, recitations, and festivals to dramatize those convictions. The ritual is a kind of illustrated textbook, and the scholar's task is to read the pictures back into the doctrine that produced them. The model has the advantage of tidiness, and it flatters the modern habit of imagining religion as primarily a matter of what one affirms.

The difficulty is that the model sits poorly with much of the evidence. Consider the pilgrimage circuits of many traditions, in which participants walk for weeks, circle shrines in prescribed directions, and bathe at designated places. When ethnographers ask walkers why they circle to the left rather than the right, the usual answer is not a doctrine but a shrug and the remark that this is how it is done. If ritual were an illustrated textbook, one would expect participants to be able to read it. Instead they perform with great exactness and little commentary, and the exactness seems to be the point.

A minority of scholars have therefore proposed reversing the order of explanation. Ritual, they argue, is the more stable element, and belief the more fluid one. Doctrines are reinterpreted every generation, abandoned in schism, and translated into new idioms, while the gestures persist almost unchanged for centuries. Communities often supply new explanations for old actions, much as a family may invent a story to account for an inherited recipe whose original purpose is forgotten. On this account, belief is frequently a retrospective gloss: people act together first, and then reach for reasons.

This reversal should not be accepted too quickly, because it inherits the tidiness of the view it replaces. To say that ritual comes first is also to offer a single arrow of causation, merely pointing the other way. The historical record contains cases in which a reforming movement altered doctrine and, within a generation, rewrote the liturgy to match; here belief plainly led. It also contains cases in which a ritual was abandoned because it came to seem incompatible with what the community thought true. Neither order of explanation can claim the field.

What the evidence supports, I think, is a more modest claim: that ritual and belief are mutually shaping, and that their relation varies with the tradition, the period, and even the individual worshipper. A participant may arrive at a festival with firm convictions, find them altered by the experience of standing among thousands, and leave with a different account of what the festival means. Another may attend for years from habit, and only under questioning discover that she holds an opinion about it. To describe both people, we need a vocabulary that does not force their experience into a sequence.

This has a practical consequence for the study of unfamiliar traditions. A researcher who assumes that practice illustrates doctrine will tend to seek out the priest, the text, and the articulate informant, and will treat the silent majority as imperfectly informed. A researcher who assumes the reverse will do the opposite, and risk dismissing the sophisticated theology that many communities do possess. The wiser course is to treat each as a hypothesis to be tested against the particular case, remaining alert to the possibility that the participants themselves have never settled the matter, and have no need to.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.A: Ritual precedes belief, and doctrines are mostly after-the-fact rationalizations of communal practice, so texts deserve little attention.
options.B: Ethnographers should rely on priests and texts because ordinary worshippers cannot explain what they do, and observation adds little.
options.C: Neither the claim that ritual expresses belief nor the claim that belief follows ritual adequately describes the relation, which is better treated as variable and mutual.
options.D: Modern readers misunderstand religion because they emphasize what is affirmed rather than what is performed, and should study only ritual.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author critiques both causal orders and ends by endorsing a mutual, context-dependent relation. Why the others are wrong: A) The author presents this as a reversal that should not be accepted too quickly. B) The author warns that this strategy risks misjudging silent participants, and also notes the opposite error. D) This is a side remark about the appeal of the older model, not the passage's thesis.
questions.trap: Picking the reversal view because it receives sympathetic, detailed treatment in the middle of the passage; the author rejects it as one-sided too.

questions.stem: The author mentions pilgrims who answer questions about circling direction with a shrug in order to:

options.A: demonstrate that pilgrims are ignorant of their own religion and should therefore be ignored by researchers.
options.B: prove that the direction of circling has no real significance for the tradition or for the people who follow it.
options.C: show that participants often perform exactly without being able to supply doctrinal explanations.
options.D: argue that ethnographers ask poorly designed questions of worshippers and should adopt better methods of interviewing.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The shrug illustrates exact performance without commentary, which strains the illustrated-textbook model. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not call pilgrims ignorant; the point concerns the model, not the pilgrims. B) Exactness is described as the point, so the direction is plainly significant to them. D) No criticism of ethnographic questions is offered.
questions.trap: Reading the shrug as evidence of ignorance or insignificance rather than as evidence about how practice and explanation relate.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true of the view that belief is a retrospective gloss on ritual?

options.A: It offers a single direction of causation, just as the view it replaces does.
options.B: It is contradicted by every historical case in which doctrine changed.
options.C: It is supported by cases in which liturgy was rewritten after a reform.
options.D: It was first proposed by the scholars who defended the illustrated-textbook model.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The fourth paragraph says the reversal merely points the arrow the other way. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says it fits some cases and fails in others, not that every case contradicts it. C) Liturgy rewritten after doctrinal reform is cited as a case where belief led. D) The reversal is proposed by a minority opposed to the older model.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing from the counterexample cases to claim they refute the view entirely.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the relation between ritual and belief varies across traditions?

options.A: Some worshippers attend festivals for years before forming any opinion about them, and then adopt the opinions of their neighbors.
options.B: Across a large sample of traditions and periods, doctrine changed first in virtually every documented case of liturgical change.
options.C: Several communities invent new explanations for inherited gestures whose origins are forgotten, while continuing to perform the gestures unchanged.
options.D: Some ritual practices were abandoned in particular communities because they seemed inconsistent with the truths those communities accepted.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) A uniform order across traditions would undercut the claim of variation and favor the older model. Why the others are wrong: A) This is consistent with the author's examples and does not threaten variation. C) The author already cites this and it fits the variation claim. D) The author cites this as a case where belief led, consistent with variation.
questions.trap: Selecting a statement already used as supporting evidence in the passage rather than one that challenges the conclusion.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the illustrated-textbook model is best described as:

options.A: dismissive and contemptuous of its proponents.
options.B: enthusiastic, with minor reservations about its method.
options.C: indifferent, treating it as equal to its rival.
options.D: critical but acknowledging its appeal.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author grants its tidiness and flattery of modern habits, yet argues it fits poorly with evidence. Why the others are wrong: A) The tone is measured and concedes advantages. B) The author rejects the model as inadequate, not as nearly right. C) The author finds both models inadequate but does not treat them as equals in the pilgrimage evidence.
questions.trap: Mistaking sustained disagreement for scorn when the author actually credits the model's advantages.

questions.stem: Suppose a researcher studying a village festival finds that residents readily describe its theology in detail yet cannot explain several of its gestures. This finding would be most consistent with:

options.A: the author's view that the relation between practice and belief may differ even within one tradition.
options.B: the claim that ritual is simply an illustrated textbook of doctrine, in which gestures merely repeat what believers already affirm.
options.C: the claim that sophisticated theology is absent from communities that perform exact rituals, since exact performance requires no reflection.
options.D: the claim that belief is always a retrospective gloss on practice, invented afterward by participants to explain what they already do.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Mixed articulacy fits the author's picture of varying, mutually shaping relations. Why the others are wrong: B) If gestures cannot be explained, the textbook reading fails for them. C) The researcher found detailed theology, so this is contradicted. D) Detailed theology existing alongside unexplained gestures does not show belief is always a gloss.
questions.trap: Treating a partial confirmation of the older model as full confirmation of one side, ignoring the mixed evidence.

passages.passage_text:
Legal systems are often praised for their rationality, yet they have always relied on fictions: statements that the law treats as true while knowing them to be false. A corporation is a "person" that can sue and be sued. A child found abandoned is "deemed" to have been born in the place where she was found. In older English practice, a plaintiff seeking access to a court that did not hear his sort of claim would allege that the defendant had trespassed, whether or not any trespass had occurred, so that the court could take jurisdiction. The defendant was not permitted to deny the allegation. Critics from Bentham onward have found such devices embarrassing, and have urged that a rational system say what it means.

The critics are right that fictions can conceal. When a court pretends that a seller always knew of a defect, it may obscure the actual policy choice, which is that sellers ought to bear the cost of defects they are better placed to discover. A false statement placed in the middle of an opinion invites later judges to take it literally and to draw conclusions that its inventors never intended.

Yet the more careful defenders of fictions observe that they do work that plain speech cannot easily do. Law faces a standing problem of adaptation. Its rules are inherited from circumstances that no longer exist, and its institutions cannot simply rewrite them whenever they seem unsuited to the present. Legislatures act slowly, and judges are constrained by precedent and by their own claims to apply rather than make law. A fiction permits a court to preserve the verbal form of an old rule while altering its effect, so that continuity is maintained even as substance changes. The corporation-as-person device, for instance, allowed courts to extend familiar rules about contracts and property to new organizations without first drafting a comprehensive code for them.

It is tempting to conclude that fictions are therefore a harmless convenience, a kind of lubricant for the machinery. But this conclusion also moves too quickly. A lubricant is invisible when it works, and a fiction that remains in use long after its purpose has lapsed becomes a source of friction rather than relief. Legal history records many such cases, in which a formula devised to avoid a harsh rule survived the repeal of that rule and continued to produce odd results because no one remembered what it had been meant to avoid.

One way of reconciling the two positions is to distinguish between fictions that are transparent and those that are opaque. A transparent fiction is one that all parties understand to be a convention, as when a jurist says "let us treat the company as a person for this purpose." Its falsity is acknowledged, and so its limits are visible: everyone knows that the company cannot be imprisoned or married. An opaque fiction, by contrast, is believed, or at least not examined, and it tends to expand beyond the purpose for which it was created. The practical lesson is not that fictions should be abolished, but that they should be made to carry labels, and that courts should periodically ask whether the problem they were invented to solve still exists.

Such a standard would not satisfy a thoroughgoing rationalist, who would prefer that every rule justify itself in the language of its actual purpose. But the demand for perfect candor underestimates how much of social life depends on useful pretenses, and how often the alternative to a fiction is not truth but paralysis.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: evaluate criticisms of legal fictions and propose a way of keeping their benefits while limiting their costs.
options.B: trace the history of corporate personhood from early English practice to the present and show how its legal uses have steadily expanded.
options.C: argue that legal systems should abandon fictions in favor of plain statements of policy, since candor always serves the public better.
options.D: show that judges invent fictions mainly to expand their own authority, and that legislatures should therefore take over the practice.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author weighs the critics and defenders and then recommends transparency and periodic review. Why the others are wrong: B) Corporate personhood is only one example among several. C) The author rejects the rationalist demand for perfect candor. D) The passage says nothing about judicial self-aggrandizement; fictions are tied to adaptation.
questions.trap: Taking a prominent example as the subject of the whole passage.

questions.stem: In the passage, the example of the defendant who could not deny an alleged trespass serves to illustrate:

options.A: a fiction that was transparent because all parties understood it as a convention.
options.B: a case in which a court deliberately punished an innocent party in order to secure a harsh rule's intended effect.
options.C: a fiction that survived because legislators could not repeal it, even after its original purpose had been forgotten.
options.D: a fiction used to give a court jurisdiction over claims it would not otherwise hear.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The allegation was false but allowed the court to take jurisdiction, and the defendant could not contest it. Why the others are wrong: A) The defendant was forbidden to deny it, which fits an opaque rather than transparent device. B) The passage does not describe punishment of an innocent party. C) Nothing is said about legislative repeal in this example.
questions.trap: Assuming a fiction that is formally accepted by everyone is transparent; transparency requires acknowledged falsity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly implied by the author's discussion of the corporation-as-person device?

options.A: Corporations should be treated as persons for every purpose, including imprisonment, because the fiction reflects what they actually are.
options.B: The device is now an example of an opaque fiction that should be dropped, because courts have forgotten that it is only a convenience.
options.C: Legislatures have never been able to regulate corporations, which is why courts were forced to develop the fiction on their own.
options.D: Treating organizations as persons let courts reuse existing rules without first writing a new code.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The third paragraph states that it extended familiar rules to new organizations without a comprehensive code. Why the others are wrong: A) The author notes that a company cannot be imprisoned or married. B) The author uses it as a transparent example, not as one to drop. C) The passage says legislatures act slowly, not that they cannot regulate.
questions.trap: Treating a helpful device as endorsed without limit.

questions.stem: The author claims that a fiction that lingers after its purpose has lapsed becomes a source of friction. Which of the following would most support this claim?

options.A: A formula designed to evade a harsh rule continues to yield odd outcomes after that rule has been repealed.
options.B: A court openly states that it is treating a company as a person for a limited purpose, and explains the convenience that justifies doing so.
options.C: A legislature replaces a fiction with a detailed statute that states its purpose, so that courts no longer need to pretend anything.
options.D: A fiction is abandoned once judges recognize that the problem it solved has disappeared, and the old formula is dropped without comment.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This directly matches the surviving formula that produces odd results. Why the others are wrong: B) This is a transparent fiction functioning as intended. C) This is an alternative to fictions, not evidence of friction from a lingering one. D) This shows the successful removal of a fiction, which gives no evidence of friction.
questions.trap: Choosing a case showing a fiction working well rather than one persisting beyond its purpose.

questions.stem: The author would most likely respond to a rationalist who demands that every rule be justified in the language of its actual purpose by arguing that:

options.A: fictions are in fact more truthful than direct statements of policy, because they reveal how judges actually reason about hard cases.
options.B: only legislatures should be permitted to use fictions, since they alone are accountable to the public for what the fictions conceal.
options.C: citizens benefit from not knowing the real rationale of rules, because open discussion of that rationale weakens respect for law.
options.D: perfect candor is not always attainable, and the real alternative to a fiction is sometimes stalled adaptation.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The final sentence says the alternative to fiction is often paralysis, not truth. Why the others are wrong: A) The author concedes fictions are false statements. B) The passage does not restrict fictions to legislatures. C) The author acknowledges that fictions can conceal the real policy choice and does not praise ignorance.
questions.trap: Overstating the author's defense into a claim that fictions are good in themselves.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best description of the author's distinction between transparent and opaque fictions?

options.A: A transparent fiction is written into statute and thereby approved by legislators, while an opaque one appears only in judicial opinions.
options.B: A transparent fiction acknowledges its own falsity and thereby reveals its limits, while an opaque one is taken as true and tends to spread.
options.C: A transparent fiction is always harmless to the parties before the court, while an opaque one always causes a clear injustice.
options.D: A transparent fiction serves questions of jurisdiction in the courts, while an opaque one serves only the law of property and inheritance.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This restates the fifth paragraph's contrast of acknowledged versus unexamined fictions. Why the others are wrong: A) The source of the fiction is not the basis of the distinction. C) The author says opaque fictions tend to expand, not that all cause injustice or that transparent ones never fail. D) Subject matter plays no role in the distinction.
questions.trap: Importing a distinction by source or subject matter instead of by whether falsity is acknowledged.

passages.passage_text:
Few arts are as stubbornly resistant to preservation as dance. A painting hangs on a wall, a poem sits on a page, a symphony is captured in a score that any trained musician can realize. A dance, by contrast, seems to vanish in the instant of its performance, leaving only memory in the bodies of those who danced it. For centuries this impermanence was treated as the essence of the form, and choreographers took a certain pride in working in a medium that could not be hoarded.

Yet efforts to notate movement are old. Renaissance dancing masters devised shorthand for the steps of court dances, and in the twentieth century several comprehensive systems were developed, some using abstract symbols arranged on a staff that records the direction, level, and duration of each movement. Advocates argued that notation would give dance what music had long possessed: a text, independent of any particular performer, from which works could be revived and studied. Libraries now hold notated scores of major ballets, and some companies stage works on the strength of the score alone.

The results have been mixed, and the reasons are instructive. A musical score succeeds because music has a relatively small set of dimensions, pitch and duration chief among them, that can be written down with great precision, and because performers are trained in a shared set of conventions for supplying the rest. A dancer's body, however, moves in many dimensions at once, and the qualities that audiences value most, the weight of a step, the arc of a gesture, the timing of a breath, are the very qualities that notation captures least well. A score may specify that an arm rises to shoulder height over two beats and say nothing about whether the rise is a surrender or a challenge. Two companies working from the same score can produce performances that look like different works.

Some conclude from this that notation has failed and that dance can only be passed from body to body. That conclusion is too sweeping, and it rests on a mistaken comparison. The fair comparison is not between a score and a performance but between a dance score and the way that works are actually transmitted in the absence of one. Without notation, a choreographer's work is carried by a single repetiteur, or by a handful of dancers who remember it, and it changes with each retelling. Details drift, steps are simplified to suit new bodies, and a work can be lost entirely within a generation when its keepers retire. Notation, imperfect as it is, serves as a check against such drift, since it fixes what can be fixed, and gives later interpreters something to argue with.

This suggests a more productive way to think about the dance score. It is less like a recording than like a legal constitution: a document that constrains without determining, that must be interpreted by successive generations, and that remains authoritative precisely because it does not settle every question. Its value lies not in making performances identical but in making the disagreements among them legible. When a company departs from the score, it can do so knowingly, and the audience that cares to look can see where the departure occurred.

On this view, the old pride in dance as an unhoardable art may be only half right. Dance is fleeting, but the fleetingness is not total, and the arts of memory, whether in the body or on the page, have always worked together.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the author's position on dance notation?

options.A: Notation cannot fully capture dance, but it provides a useful constraint on drift and makes departures from a work visible.
options.B: Notation has failed as a method of preservation because it cannot record qualities such as weight and timing, and should be abandoned.
options.C: Notation makes dance as permanent and reproducible as a musical score, so that performances no longer depend on the memories of dancers.
options.D: Notation is unnecessary because dancers transmit works reliably from body to body, with little change across successive generations of performers.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author concedes limits yet defends notation as a check and an object of interpretation. Why the others are wrong: B) The author calls this conclusion too sweeping. C) The author says notation is imperfect and that performances may look like different works. D) The author describes oral transmission as prone to drift and loss.
questions.trap: Treating the acknowledged limits as the author's conclusion rather than as a concession.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a musical score is more effective than a dance score for which of the following reasons?

options.A: Musicians are more disciplined than dancers about following written instructions, and therefore depart less from what a score prescribes.
options.B: Musical notation was invented centuries earlier than any system for dance, and has had far more time to become a standard.
options.C: Music is not subject to differences between performances, because a score completely determines every aspect of how it is played.
options.D: Music has fewer dimensions that must be specified and performers share conventions for supplying the rest.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The third paragraph says music has few dimensions that can be written precisely, plus shared conventions. Why the others are wrong: A) Discipline is not discussed. B) Renaissance dance notations are mentioned; chronology is not the explanation. C) Different performances of the same score obviously exist, and the passage does not deny this.
questions.trap: Substituting a plausible but unmentioned explanation about performer attitude.

questions.stem: The author compares the dance score to a legal constitution in order to:

options.A: argue that dance companies are obligated by law to follow scores exactly, and may be penalized for any deviation.
options.B: suggest that a score constrains without determining, and gains authority by requiring interpretation.
options.C: imply that choreographers should resolve every disagreement before a performance, so that interpretation is never needed.
options.D: claim that dance scores are more precise than constitutional text, and therefore leave less room for interpretation.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The analogy stresses constraint without determination and successive interpretation. Why the others are wrong: A) The comparison is figurative, not about legal obligations. C) The author says value lies in making disagreements legible, not in eliminating them. D) The author says precision is limited; the analogy concerns interpretation.
questions.trap: Reading the analogy literally as a claim about enforcement.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about works transmitted without notation?

options.A: They are more likely to change as they pass through successive keepers.
options.B: They are always performed identically by every company, because the steps are fixed once they have been taught to the first dancers.
options.C: They are valued more by audiences than notated works, since viewers prefer performances that depend on the memory of living dancers.
options.D: They cannot be revived once the last dancer who learned them has retired, because no other form of record can exist.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author describes drift, simplification, and loss without a notated check. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says details drift, the opposite of identity. C) Audience preference is not discussed. D) The passage says works may be lost, not that revival is impossible in every case.
questions.trap: Stretching 'can be lost' to 'cannot be revived' in all cases.

questions.stem: Which of the following would most weaken the author's argument that notation acts as a check against drift?

options.A: Two companies using the same score produce performances that look different from each other.
options.B: Libraries hold scores of major ballets that are rarely consulted.
options.C: Companies working from notated scores alter the works as much as companies relying on memory do.
options.D: Some choreographers prefer that their works not be preserved.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) If notation reduced no more drift than memory, the claimed checking function would be undermined. Why the others are wrong: A) The author already grants this and still says the score fixes what can be fixed. B) Rare consultation does not show that consulted scores fail to constrain. D) Choreographer preferences do not bear on whether notation checks drift.
questions.trap: Choosing a point the author already concedes instead of one that attacks the check-on-drift claim itself.

questions.stem: The final paragraph suggests that the pride in dance as an 'unhoardable art' is:

options.A: entirely justified, since notation cannot preserve anything essential about a work and dance therefore disappears with each performance.
options.B: entirely mistaken, since dance is as permanent as painting once it has been recorded in any form, whether notated or remembered.
options.C: partly justified, since dance is fleeting, but overstated since memory in body and page can preserve some of it.
options.D: irrelevant to the choice between memory and written scores, since the permanence of an art form has no bearing on how it is kept.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says the view is 'only half right' because the fleetingness is not total. Why the others are wrong: A) The author denies that notation preserves nothing. B) The author does not claim dance equals painting in permanence. D) The author connects the pride to the role of memory arts, not dismisses it as irrelevant.
questions.trap: Taking 'half right' to mean either all right or all wrong.

passages.passage_text:
When a farmer's plow turns up a bronze vessel, or a construction crew breaks into a burial chamber, the object that emerges is already half transformed. It has been removed from the soil that surrounded it, and with that removal has gone much of what an archaeologist would most like to know: what lay beside it, at what depth, in what arrangement, and in association with what other remains. A vessel in a museum case may be admired as a work of craft, but as evidence it is nearly mute. This is why archaeologists insist, sometimes to the annoyance of collectors, that the context of an artifact is more valuable than the artifact itself.

The claim is easy to misunderstand. It does not say that objects are unimportant, nor that a beautiful piece has no value to scholarship. Its point is that knowledge in archaeology is produced by relations rather than by things. A single coin found in a layer of ash tells almost nothing, but the same coin found beneath a collapsed roof, above a floor of beaten earth, and beside a hoard of similar coins can date a destruction, identify a trade route, and suggest the wealth of a household. The information lies in the pattern, and the pattern is destroyed when any element is extracted without record.

This principle underlies the strong condemnation of looting, which strips sites of objects for the antiquities market. Defenders of the market sometimes reply that museums and private collectors preserve objects that would otherwise decay or be lost, and that many looted pieces are now better cared for than they would have been in the ground. The reply has force as far as the object is concerned. But it overlooks the fact that the loss imposed by looting is not primarily a loss of objects. A looted tomb may yield a handsome pot, while the scholar's chance of learning who was buried there, and how the community regarded the dead, is permanently reduced.

Yet an insistence on context can itself become a dogma, and some archaeologists have begun to question its more absolute forms. Excavation is destructive. Every trench removes the very layers that it records, and the record that remains is a product of the excavator's choices about what to notice and what to ignore. Early excavators discarded animal bones and seeds that modern specialists consider invaluable, and recorded nothing about soil that is now routinely analyzed chemically. If context is the true repository of meaning, then a careless modern excavation may be no better, in principle, than a plunderer's, since both destroy what the next generation might have read with better tools.

This is not a reason to abandon excavation, but it does recommend humility. Context is not a fixed quantity waiting to be recovered; it is something that is defined by the questions currently asked of it. Which features count as relevant evidence changes as methods change, and the excavator therefore acts not only as a reader of the past but as a custodian whose decisions bind later readers. Responsible practice means leaving portions of a site untouched whenever the research aim permits, and keeping records detailed enough to allow future scholars to evaluate the interpretations built from them.

The ethical weight of the principle is thus double. It condemns the person who destroys context for profit, and it also disciplines the professional who destroys context for knowledge, by reminding both that a site can be excavated only once.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

options.A: arguing that museums should return looted objects to their countries of origin, regardless of how the objects were acquired.
options.B: explaining why context matters more than objects in archaeology and what responsibilities follow from this.
options.C: showing that early excavators were more careless than modern ones, and that the discipline has improved steadily as methods advanced.
options.D: defending the antiquities market against charges of causing destruction, since collectors preserve objects that would otherwise be lost.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage develops the principle, applies it to looting, and extends it to excavators. Why the others are wrong: A) Repatriation is never discussed. C) Early excavators are an illustration, not the subject. D) The market's defense is acknowledged and then answered.
questions.trap: Focusing on the looting discussion because it is the most emotionally charged part, rather than the full argument.

questions.stem: The example of the coin found beneath a collapsed roof is used to show that:

options.A: coins are the most informative kind of artifact, because they can be dated by the inscriptions and rulers they carry.
options.B: a destruction layer can be dated only by coins, since no other objects found at a site can fix a date.
options.C: wealthy households are always identifiable from hoards, because only the rich owned enough valuables to bury them.
options.D: the information in a find depends on its relations to surrounding features.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The same coin gains meaning from its associations. Why the others are wrong: A) The coin is just an example, with no ranking of artifact types. B) The passage says coins can help date, not that only coins can. C) The passage says the pattern 'suggests' wealth, not that hoards always identify it.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing a single illustration into a universal rule.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the reply of the market's defenders is limited because it:

options.A: is contradicted by evidence that looted objects are poorly cared for once they have been removed from the ground and sold.
options.B: addresses the physical survival of objects but not the loss of information about their context.
options.C: wrongly assumes that archaeologists value objects too little, when in fact they care only about the objects themselves.
options.D: ignores the fact that museums are not interested in beauty, and so cannot be trusted to protect the finest objects.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author grants it has force for objects but says the real loss is contextual. Why the others are wrong: A) The author grants that the objects may be better cared for. C) The author says archaeologists do value objects, as the earlier paragraph shows. D) Beauty is not at issue.
questions.trap: Assuming the author denies the factual claim when she in fact accepts it and challenges its relevance.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about the claim that 'context is the true repository of meaning'?

options.A: It was abandoned by archaeologists once chemical analysis of soil became routine, because such analysis made context unnecessary to record.
options.B: Because what counts as context changes with methods, the claim cannot justify treating current practice as final.
options.C: It implies that excavation should never occur, since any digging destroys information that later researchers might be able to read.
options.D: It applies to looters but not to professional excavators, since professionals are trained to recognize and preserve every kind of evidence.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says context is defined by current questions and therefore recommends humility. Why the others are wrong: A) The author keeps the principle and refines it. C) The author says this is not a reason to abandon excavation. D) The final paragraph applies the principle to both groups.
questions.trap: Concluding that a criticism of absolutism is a rejection of the principle altogether.

questions.stem: Which of the following new findings would most support the author's point about the excavator as custodian?

options.A: A looted vessel is shown to have been well maintained in a private collection and to have been kept free of damage for decades.
options.B: A dig team finds a coin beside a hoard of similar coins and dates the whole group of objects to a single reign.
options.C: A site is protected by law from all excavation, so that no future team can recover information that present methods cannot detect.
options.D: Seeds discarded in a past excavation are later shown to indicate the diet of the people who lived at the site.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Discarded material later proving valuable shows how decisions bind later readers. Why the others are wrong: A) This supports the market's defenders' point about objects, not the custodian point. B) This reflects the importance of association, not later reinterpretation. C) Complete protection is not what the author recommends; she urges leaving portions untouched where aims permit.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about context in general rather than evidence about how excavators' choices affect later scholars.

questions.stem: The author's concluding sentence suggests that the principle:

options.A: applies to professional excavators as well as to looters, because excavation is unrepeatable.
options.B: exempts professionals because they record what they remove, so that no information is lost when a layer is dug away.
options.C: is irrelevant where sites have been excavated more than once, since repeated digging provides the missing context for every find.
options.D: should be replaced by a principle that values objects over context, since objects are the only finds that museums can display.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) A site can be excavated only once, so both parties destroy context. Why the others are wrong: B) The fourth paragraph says careless modern excavation may be no better in principle. C) The sentence asserts that a site can be excavated only once. D) The author does not endorse valuing objects over context.
questions.trap: Letting professional purpose excuse the destruction the author says both groups cause.

passages.passage_text:
Theories of civil disobedience usually begin by distinguishing it from ordinary lawbreaking. The civil disobedient, we are told, acts publicly, accepts the legal consequences of her act, and appeals to a shared sense of justice rather than to private advantage. She breaks a law in order to draw attention to its wrongness, and her willingness to be punished is meant to show that she respects the legal order even as she challenges one of its parts. The most influential versions of this account, developed in the twentieth century, add that the disobedience should be nonviolent and should come only after legal avenues of reform have been tried and have failed.

This picture has a clear moral logic. It reconciles the demand that citizens obey the law with the recognition that majorities sometimes enact injustice. By accepting punishment, the protester signals that she does not regard herself as exempt from the rules that bind others, and by acting openly, she invites her fellow citizens to evaluate her claim. The act becomes a form of address, a speech delivered in the language of conduct to an audience that has not been persuaded by words.

But the standard account has been criticized for presupposing a society in which the legal order is basically just and responsive. Where a government systematically excludes a group from the political process, the requirement that protesters first exhaust legal avenues amounts to telling them to petition an authority that has no obligation to listen. Likewise, the insistence on accepting punishment assumes that courts will treat the disobedient fairly. If sentences are used to silence a movement, submission to them may serve the repression rather than the protest. Critics conclude that the conditions of the standard account describe a particular kind of political circumstance, namely a reasonably healthy liberal democracy, and not a universal ethics of dissent.

Defenders of the standard account have two replies. First, they say, the conditions are not meant to be applied mechanically, but to mark the conduct that is most clearly justified, leaving other forms of protest to be judged by other standards. A theory that identifies the central case does not claim that everything outside it is wrong. Second, they argue that the conditions have a strategic rationale that survives imperfect circumstances. A protest that is public, nonviolent, and accepting of penalty is hard to portray as mere criminality, and thus it keeps the sympathy of bystanders whom a more aggressive tactic would alienate.

The second reply, however, depends on an empirical assumption about how audiences respond, and the assumption is not always borne out. Authorities have repeatedly succeeded in labeling peaceful protest as disorder, while some disruptive campaigns have won public support by the evident gravity of their cause. The strategic defense, then, is a hypothesis about particular audiences rather than a general truth, and it must be tested case by case.

What may be learned from this dispute is that the standard account is best read as an ideal type, describing what dissent looks like when circumstances are favorable, and offering a vocabulary for assessing departures from it. To insist that it either governs all cases or none misconceives the kind of claim it makes. A map of a well-surveyed region is no less useful for failing to cover the whole continent, so long as one does not mistake its borders for the edge of the world.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose is to:

options.A: assess criticisms of the standard account of civil disobedience and argue that it is best treated as an ideal type.
options.B: prove that civil disobedience is justified only in liberal democracies, where the legal order is fair enough to deserve respect.
options.C: argue that nonviolence is strategically superior to disruptive protest, because it wins more public support and sympathy for a cause.
options.D: show that accepting punishment is an essential component of any justified dissent, however unjust the system that imposes the penalty.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author evaluates criticism and two defenses, then proposes the ideal-type reading. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says the account describes conditions in such societies, not that disobedience is justified only there. C) The author calls the strategic claim a hypothesis that must be tested. D) The author questions whether accepting punishment is always appropriate.
questions.trap: Treating the critics' position as the author's own.

questions.stem: According to the standard account, the willingness of the protester to accept punishment serves to:

options.A: persuade courts to reduce the severity of sentences, since judges look more favorably on those who do not resist arrest.
options.B: demonstrate that her cause has majority support, because willingness to bear a penalty shows that many others share her view.
options.C: signal respect for the legal order even as she challenges part of it.
options.D: avoid the need for further protest once her act has been made known to the public.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The first paragraph says it shows respect for the legal order. Why the others are wrong: A) Leniency is not mentioned. B) Support is not shown by accepting punishment. D) Further protest is not discussed in this connection.
questions.trap: Importing a practical motive for a symbolic act.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the strategic defense described in the fourth paragraph?

options.A: Peaceful protests that accept penalties are frequently dismissed by the public as the work of criminals.
options.B: Disruptive campaigns sometimes lose public support, particularly when their tactics inconvenience people who are indifferent to the cause.
options.C: Courts occasionally treat protesters fairly, even when the laws that the protesters broke were passed by large majorities of voters.
options.D: Nonviolent protests are generally less expensive to organize, which explains why they are more common than disruptive campaigns.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The defense says such protest is hard to portray as criminality; contrary evidence undermines it. Why the others are wrong: B) This weakens the case for disruption, not the strategic defense of the standard conduct. C) Fair courts do not bear on audience response. D) Cost is not part of the defense.
questions.trap: Selecting evidence about disruptive protest, which supports rather than weakens the defense.

questions.stem: The author's reference to a map of a well-surveyed region serves to:

options.A: suggest that the standard account is geographically limited to certain countries.
options.B: imply that critics have misread the facts of particular protests.
options.C: indicate that a theory may be valuable within a domain without governing all cases.
options.D: argue that theories of dissent should be replaced by detailed case studies.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The map analogy makes the point about a model's useful but bounded scope. Why the others are wrong: A) The domain is conditions, not literal geography. B) The analogy concerns the nature of the theory, not factual misreading. D) The author keeps the theory as an ideal type.
questions.trap: Reading the map metaphor literally.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author most likely agree with?

options.A: A protest that departs from the standard conditions is not thereby shown to be unjustified.
options.B: Any protest that breaks the law is justified if its cause is just, whatever means are used and whoever may be harmed.
options.C: Legal avenues should never be exhausted before protest begins, because delay always makes the underlying injustice worse than the lawbreaking.
options.D: Protesters who flee punishment forfeit all moral standing, and nothing they say afterward deserves to be taken seriously by others.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Defenders and the author treat the conditions as marking the central case, with departures judged by other standards. Why the others are wrong: B) The author does not endorse such a sweeping claim. C) The author does not reject the exhaustion condition; she questions its universality. D) No such claim is made.
questions.trap: Hearing a rejection of strict conditions as endorsement of no conditions.

questions.stem: The criticism in the third paragraph depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: That protesters in unjust societies never have access to courts, so that the standard account cannot apply to them at all.
options.B: That the conditions of the standard account presuppose institutions that are fair and responsive.
options.C: That nonviolence is always ineffective under repressive regimes, because such governments respond only to threats of force.
options.D: That majorities never enact unjust laws, so that the standard account describes only protests against rules that are fair.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The critics say the account presupposes a basically just and responsive order. Why the others are wrong: A) The critics say courts may be unfair, not that access is always absent. C) Effectiveness of nonviolence is not their claim. D) The first paragraph already grants that majorities sometimes enact injustice.
questions.trap: Making the critics' claim absolute when they reason from specific circumstances.

passages.passage_text:
A common complaint about modern poetry is that it is difficult, and the complaint is often delivered with the suspicion that the difficulty is a pose. Why should a poem not say plainly what it means? The question assumes that a poem's meaning can be stated in other words, that beneath the imagery and syntax lies a message which a more forthright writer would simply have delivered. If this were so, difficulty would indeed be a kind of dishonesty, a withholding of something the poet could have handed over.

Poets and critics have long resisted this assumption. In a well-known formulation, a poem should not mean but be, which is to say that its significance is inseparable from the particular words, rhythms, and silences in which it is embodied. Paraphrase is possible, as every teacher knows, but the paraphrase is to the poem as a map is to a landscape: useful for orientation, incapable of being walked through. To ask what a poem means in other words is already to have changed the subject, since the experience that the poem provides is not a conclusion arrived at by a route that might be shortened.

This defense, though, can be pushed too far. If poems cannot be paraphrased at all, nothing can be said about them, and criticism becomes pointless. Readers do discuss poems, agree on interpretations, and sometimes persuade one another that a reading is mistaken. The truth appears to be that paraphrase is possible but partial: it recovers some of what a poem does while necessarily losing the rest. What distinguishes a poem from an essay is not that it has no paraphrasable content but that the content is not its chief achievement, which lies in how the content is held.

Consider the effect of line breaks. A poet who ends a line in the middle of a sentence creates a small pause that does not exist in prose, and in that pause a reader may entertain a meaning that the next line then revises. A line that reads "she left the house behind" may suggest abandonment until the following line adds "her at the window," whereupon the first meaning is not canceled but shadowed by the second. The reader experiences both, in sequence, and the resulting ambiguity is part of what the poem communicates. A paraphrase would have to choose, and in choosing would eliminate precisely the instability that the poet had arranged.

Difficulty, on this account, is not a barrier erected between the poem and the reader, but a feature of the kind of attention that the poem requires. It slows reading so that the words may be encountered as words, rather than as vehicles to be discarded on arrival. That is not to say that every obscure poem is successful. Obscurity may result from private reference that the poet failed to make accessible, or from carelessness mistaken for depth. The test is whether the reader's effort is rewarded: whether, after sustained attention, the poem yields more than its first appearance promised.

The skeptic who suspects a pose is therefore half right. Some difficulty is affected. But to treat all difficulty as affectation is to demand that poetry become a more efficient delivery system for statements, and to forget that efficiency was never the point.

questions.stem: The author's central claim about difficult poetry is that:

options.A: its difficulty is often a legitimate feature of the attention it demands, though not every obscure poem succeeds.
options.B: its difficulty is nearly always an affectation by poets who wish to appear profound, and readers are right to dismiss it.
options.C: its meaning cannot be discussed or paraphrased in any form, so critics can offer readers no help in approaching it.
options.D: it should be simplified so that readers can reach its message more quickly, since efficiency is the proper goal of reading.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author defends difficulty as a feature while admitting that obscurity may fail. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says the skeptic is only half right. C) The author explicitly rejects the claim that nothing can be said. D) The author argues against treating poetry as efficient delivery of statements.
questions.trap: Adopting the skeptic's view because the author concedes some difficulty is affected.

questions.stem: In the passage, the comparison of paraphrase to a map is used to suggest that paraphrase:

options.A: is useful for orientation but cannot reproduce the experience of the poem itself.
options.B: is deceptive and should be avoided by careful readers, since any restatement of a poem in plain terms misleads its audience.
options.C: is more accurate than the poem because it is clearer, and so is the better guide to what the poet meant.
options.D: can substitute for the poem when time is limited, since the plain statement carries all that the poem communicates.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) A map orients but cannot be walked through. Why the others are wrong: B) The author calls it useful. C) Clarity is not equated with accuracy to the poem's achievement. D) The author says it cannot capture the experience.
questions.trap: Treating a limited tool as a worthless one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the line 'she left the house behind' followed by 'her at the window' illustrates that:

options.A: poets should avoid ending a line mid-sentence, because such breaks interrupt the reader and make the sense harder to follow.
options.B: the second line corrects an error in the first, so that the reader must discard the first meaning entirely.
options.C: a line break can allow a first meaning to be shadowed rather than canceled by a second.
options.D: ambiguity in poetry is always unintentional, and readers should resolve it by choosing whichever meaning is the most common.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says both meanings are experienced in sequence. Why the others are wrong: A) The author presents the effect as a poetic resource. B) The first meaning is shadowed, not corrected as an error. D) The author says the poet arranged the instability.
questions.trap: Reading revision as correction rather than layering.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that a criticism that insists a poem 'cannot be discussed' is:

options.A: correct, since poems are inseparable from their words and no two readers can ever arrive at the same understanding of one.
options.B: correct, since paraphrase always distorts a poem and therefore no interpretation can be better or worse than another.
options.C: irrelevant, since poems do not communicate anything to readers and so cannot be understood in the first place.
options.D: mistaken, since readers do reach shared interpretations and correct one another.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The third paragraph rejects this extreme. Why the others are wrong: A) Inseparability does not mean silence on the subject. B) Paraphrase is partial, not useless. C) The author says poems communicate through ambiguity.
questions.trap: Following the first half of the defense without noting its limit.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as a justified criticism of a poem?

options.A: The poem rewards repeated reading with new layers of meaning that were not evident on the first encounter.
options.B: The poem depends on a private reference that readers cannot recover, so sustained attention yields nothing more.
options.C: The poem contains a line break that produces ambiguity, so that two meanings are held together at once.
options.D: The poem cannot be paraphrased in full, and the reader's sense of it changes as the poem is reread.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author names inaccessible private reference and unrewarded effort as failures. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the success test. C) This is praised as a poetic effect. D) Partial paraphrasability is expected of poems.
questions.trap: Confusing difficulty itself with the kind of difficulty the author criticizes.

questions.stem: The final paragraph's reference to efficiency suggests that the skeptic's demand rests on the view that poetry should be:

options.A: entirely free of rhythm and imagery, since such features distract from the message that is being conveyed.
options.B: written only by trained critics, who alone are able to decide what a given text is supposed to communicate.
options.C: read only by those who already understand it, since no one else could be expected to follow its meaning.
options.D: a means of transmitting statements as quickly as possible.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says the skeptic would turn poetry into a delivery system for statements. Why the others are wrong: A) Rhythm and imagery are not the target. B) Authorship is not discussed. C) Readership limits are not discussed.
questions.trap: Choosing an option about form rather than purpose.

passages.passage_text:
The arrival of synchronized sound in the late 1920s is conventionally told as a story of progress: silent film was a promising but incomplete art, and the talkies completed it. The story is so familiar that it is easy to overlook how many of the period's filmmakers and critics regarded the change as a catastrophe. They did not object to sound as such. Their complaint was that early sound technology, which required actors to speak toward concealed microphones and cameras to be sealed in soundproof booths, froze a medium that had only recently learned to move.

By the mid-1920s, silent cinema had developed a sophisticated visual grammar. Directors used the moving camera, rapid cutting, and carefully composed images to convey emotion and thought without a word of dialogue, and the intertitle, which had once been a crutch, had become in skilled hands a sparing and sometimes poetic device. Audiences had learned to read faces, gestures, and the rhythms of editing. The loss of this grammar in the first years of sound was real: films of the early talkie period are often static, dominated by people standing near a microphone and talking.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that silent film was a complete art that sound merely spoiled. Silent film was never silent; theaters employed pianists, organists, and sometimes full orchestras, and the experience of the film varied with the musicians and the audience. The "silent" form was therefore already a performance medium in which each screening differed, and its apparent purity is partly a creation of later archives, which preserve the film but not the music that accompanied it. The art that the sound-era critics mourned was in some respects an art that survives only in reconstruction.

Nor did the early limitations of sound last. Within a few years, microphones became portable, cameras were freed from their booths, and directors discovered that sound could do things that images could not. A sound heard from off screen could suggest a presence that the picture withheld; a conversation could overlap another in a way that no intertitle could represent; and silence itself, deliberately introduced into a soundtrack, could gain a force that it never had when silence was the default. Filmmakers who had mastered the visual grammar of the silent era often proved the best at exploiting these resources, since they understood that the image should continue to carry meaning even when speech was available.

The most defensible account of the transition, then, is neither a triumph nor a tragedy. It was a disruption that destroyed some achievements and made others possible, and the ledger cannot be balanced by an appeal to a single standard of artistic completeness. The idea that an art form has a destination, toward which it moves when its technology permits, is attractive, but it imposes a purpose that the artists themselves did not share. They were not completing a form; they were responding, with varying success, to the materials available.

Seen this way, the persistence of silent filmmaking as an occasional deliberate choice in later decades is not a nostalgic eccentricity. It is evidence that the capacities of the earlier form never became obsolete, only optional.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Silent cinema was a complete art that was ruined by synchronized sound, which brought nothing of value to the medium.
options.B: Early sound technology was so limiting that it should never have been adopted, and the industry would have been better without it.
options.C: The shift to sound is better understood as a disruption with both losses and gains than as either simple progress or simple decline.
options.D: Archives have distorted our understanding of the silent era by omitting images, which is why its achievements are widely misjudged.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author rejects both triumph and tragedy narratives. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says it is a mistake to call silent film a complete art spoiled by sound. B) The limits did not last, and the author notes gains. D) Archives omitted the music, not the images.
questions.trap: Identifying the main idea with the opening critics' claim rather than the author's balanced conclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, early talkie films were often static because:

options.A: directors had forgotten the visual grammar of silent film, so that scenes became static after the industry adopted sound.
options.B: actors had to speak toward hidden microphones and cameras were enclosed in soundproof booths.
options.C: audiences preferred dialogue to movement, so studios deliberately chose to keep the camera in place for speaking scenes.
options.D: intertitles had become too elaborate, so that studios required directors to replace them with spoken lines of dialogue.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The first paragraph names the microphone and booth requirements. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says directors who mastered silent grammar proved best at using sound later. C) Audience preference is not given as the reason. D) Intertitles are not blamed.
questions.trap: Blaming filmmakers' skill rather than the technology.

questions.stem: The author's point that silent film 'was never silent' primarily serves to:

options.A: argue that live musicians were better than recorded sound, and that sound film therefore marked a decline in musical quality.
options.B: show that audiences disliked silent films shown without accompaniment, which is why theaters hired musicians to perform with them.
options.C: undermine the idea that silent cinema was a pure, uniform art form.
options.D: claim that sound film is therefore not a new medium, since it simply continued the practices of silent exhibition.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The live music made each screening differ, complicating the picture of purity. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not rank live over recorded music. B) Audience dislike is not mentioned. D) The author acknowledges that sound brought new possibilities.
questions.trap: Reading a historical correction as a preference claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about the author's view of intertitles?

options.A: They were a mark of artistic failure in all silent films, because they showed that images could not tell the story alone.
options.B: They were unnecessary once the camera moved, since moving images made written explanation of the story redundant.
options.C: They were eliminated before 1920, after directors learned to tell stories entirely through gesture and framing.
options.D: They could become an effective, restrained artistic device when used skillfully.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The second paragraph says they had become sparing and sometimes poetic in skilled hands. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says they began as a crutch but could improve. B) The passage does not tie them to camera movement. C) Dates are not given and they were used into the mid-1920s.
questions.trap: Taking the 'crutch' remark as the author's final judgment.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of off-screen sound and deliberate silence most directly supports which claim?

options.A: Directors of the silent era could not adapt to sound, and their careers declined once the new technology was introduced.
options.B: Soundtracks are more important than images, because modern audiences respond more strongly to what they hear than to what they see.
options.C: Sound opened expressive possibilities that images alone could not provide.
options.D: Silence was impossible in silent film, since live music or commentary accompanied every showing of every film ever made.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) These are examples of things sound could do that images could not. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says silent-era filmmakers often adapted best. B) The author says the image should still carry meaning. D) Silence gained force only once it was deliberately introduced, not that it was impossible earlier.
questions.trap: Turning a claim about added resources into a claim about priority.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most challenge the author's argument that sound brought genuine expressive gains?

options.A: Some directors continued to make silent films for artistic reasons, even after sound had become standard in commercial cinema.
options.B: Early sound films were often static, because the recording equipment limited where actors and cameras could be placed.
options.C: Film archives preserve the images but not the original music, so modern viewers must supply accompaniment of their own choosing.
options.D: Critics of the period agreed that films with off-screen sound and overlapping speech were less expressive than silent films.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Evidence that these techniques lacked expressive worth would undercut the claim, though the author's own judgment stays contestable. Why the others are wrong: A) The author uses this as evidence that the earlier capacities remained. B) The author already grants this. C) The author cites this about archives and it does not bear on sound's gains.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact the author already accepts.

passages.passage_text:
Few features of schooling are as widely used and as little understood as the grade. A letter or number placed at the top of a paper is treated by students, parents, universities, and employers as a compact measurement of learning. It is also, for most of those who read it, a judgment: it tells them where a student stands relative to some standard, or relative to peers. Yet any teacher can testify that the same piece of work might earn different marks from different markers, or from the same marker on different days, and that a single grade often blends what the student knows with how hard she worked, how neatly she wrote, and whether she turned the assignment in on time.

Reformers have long argued that this blending makes grades poor instruments. A grade that mixes mastery with compliance, they say, tells us neither accurately, and a student who understands a subject but neglects homework may be recorded as failing it. Their remedy is to separate the components: report achievement against clearly stated standards in one place, and behaviors such as punctuality and effort in another. Schools that have adopted such systems often find that their grades become more consistent across classrooms, and that conversations with students shift from negotiating points to identifying what remains to be learned.

The reform, however, rests on an assumption that deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives: that learning can be cleanly detached from the habits that produce it. In many fields the distinction is artificial. A student who cannot meet deadlines may be unable to complete the extended projects through which advanced skills are developed, and effort may be less a separate virtue than one of the mechanisms by which knowledge is acquired. To report mastery without regard to such habits risks describing a student's current state while leaving unstated the process on which her future progress depends.

There is a further complication. The act of measuring changes the thing measured. When students know that a grade will count toward a transcript, they adjust their behavior to the grade rather than to the learning it was meant to track, a phenomenon familiar to anyone who has studied for a test by memorizing what was likely to appear on it. Standards-based reporting does not eliminate this tendency; it only relocates it. Students who are told that they must demonstrate each of thirty standards may simply learn to demonstrate thirty standards, whether or not the demonstration reflects understanding.

None of this shows that grades should be discarded. Institutions require some means of summarizing performance, and the alternatives, such as narrative evaluations, are expensive in teachers' time and difficult for outside readers to compare. The sensible position is that a grade is a communication with several audiences, and that no single design can serve all of them equally. What teachers can do is be candid about what a given grade is meant to convey, and resist the temptation to treat it as an objective fact. A mark is a summary written by a person, using criteria chosen by a person, and its authority depends on that person's willingness to explain how it was reached.

The challenge for schools is therefore less to perfect the grade than to ensure that students and families understand what it is.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the author's central view of grades?

options.A: Grades are useful summaries whose design involves unavoidable trade-offs, so their meaning must be made explicit.
options.B: Grades are inaccurate and should be replaced by narrative evaluations, since no number can summarize what a student has learned.
options.C: Grades should measure only mastery, apart from effort and behavior, because anything else corrupts the meaning of the mark.
options.D: Grades are objective facts about a student's learning, and so can be compared directly across schools and teachers.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author endorses grades with candor about their limits. Why the others are wrong: B) Narrative evaluations are called costly and hard to compare. C) The author questions the assumption that mastery can be cleanly separated. D) The author tells teachers to resist treating a grade as objective fact.
questions.trap: Choosing the reformers' position, which the author examines critically rather than adopts.

questions.stem: According to the reformers described in the passage, a student who understands a subject but neglects homework:

options.A: should be given a higher grade for understanding, since mastery of the material is the only thing a grade ought to reflect.
options.B: may be recorded as failing under a grading system that blends mastery with compliance.
options.C: will always improve if effort is graded separately, because students respond only to what is formally counted in their grades.
options.D: should be excluded from standards-based reporting, since such systems are designed only for students who comply with routines.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This is the reformers' example of the blending problem. Why the others are wrong: A) The reformers want separation, not a bonus. C) Improvement is not asserted. D) Exclusion is not discussed.
questions.trap: Confusing the problem described with the remedy.

questions.stem: The author raises the example of studying by memorizing likely test content to show that:

options.A: measurement can shift behavior toward the measure rather than the learning it was meant to track.
options.B: tests are unfair to students who memorize well, because memorization is a skill that schools ought not to reward at all.
options.C: teachers deliberately encourage memorization, since they believe that recall of facts is the highest form of understanding.
options.D: standards-based reporting prevents this kind of behavior, because students cannot adjust their efforts to a measure that is detailed.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The example illustrates adjusting to the grade, as the paragraph states. Why the others are wrong: B) Fairness is not at issue. C) Teacher intention is not mentioned. D) The author says standards-based reporting only relocates it.
questions.trap: Missing that the author sees the problem persisting under the reform.

questions.stem: The third paragraph suggests that the reformers' assumption is questionable because:

options.A: effort and punctuality are never relevant to achievement, and should be excluded from every account of how students learn.
options.B: habits such as meeting deadlines may be part of how learning is achieved in many fields.
options.C: teachers cannot measure mastery objectively, so that any grade will inevitably reflect the personal impressions of the teacher.
options.D: students with poor habits cannot learn, and so schools are justified in lowering grades for any lapse in routine.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says effort may be a mechanism of acquiring knowledge. Why the others are wrong: A) The author argues they may be relevant. C) The point concerns the detachment of habits, not measurability. D) The author says they may impede extended projects, not make learning impossible.
questions.trap: Overextending 'may be related' to 'always prevents'.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's claim that standards-based reporting only relocates the tendency to adjust behavior to the grade?

options.A: Students under both systems study mainly what is likely to be assessed, and do so with comparable levels of effort and success.
options.B: Students under standards-based reporting show deeper understanding on unfamiliar tasks than students under traditional grading.
options.C: Teachers under standards-based reporting spend more time on grading, though their students show no difference in understanding.
options.D: Grades become more consistent across classrooms under both systems, so that comparisons between teachers become more reliable.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Deeper transfer would suggest the system does change what students learn. Why the others are wrong: A) This would support the author's claim. C) Time spent does not address behavior toward the measure. D) Consistency is a separate benefit the author already grants.
questions.trap: Selecting a result that is true of the reform but does not bear on the claim.

questions.stem: The author's concluding recommendation for teachers is most consistent with which of the following?

options.A: A teacher who adopts whichever system produces the highest grades.
options.B: A teacher who refuses to assign grades.
options.C: A teacher who explains to students how a grade was reached and what it is intended to show.
options.D: A teacher who tells students their grades are objective measurements.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says authority depends on the willingness to explain. Why the others are wrong: A) Grade inflation is not discussed. B) The author says grades remain necessary. D) The author says teachers should resist treating grades as objective fact.
questions.trap: Reading the criticism of grades as support for abolishing them.

passages.passage_text:
Compilers of encyclopedias have always had to decide, before anything else, how to arrange what they know. The choice looks like a matter of convenience, but it is better understood as a claim about the nature of knowledge. Ancient and medieval compilers generally arranged their material by subject, descending from the heavens to the earth, from God to angels to humans to animals to minerals. A reader moving through such a work was meant to experience the order of creation itself, and the book's structure taught as much as its entries did. The drawback was practical: someone who wanted to learn about a single plant had to know where in the cosmic hierarchy it belonged before the book could be of any help.

The alphabetical encyclopedia solved that problem by giving up on the cosmic hierarchy. Arranged by the first letter of each heading, it required nothing of its reader except the name of the thing sought. Its early modern advocates praised it as neutral, since no one's theory of the world determined where an entry would fall. Yet neutrality had a cost. Alphabetical order scatters related topics across the volumes, so that "anatomy" and "surgery" stand far apart while "anatomy" sits beside "anchor." Knowledge, which had been a structure, became a collection of fragments.

The editors of the great eighteenth-century French Encyclopédie were acutely aware of this cost and tried to repair it with two devices. They prefaced the work with a diagram, a tree of knowledge, showing how the disciplines were thought to descend from the human faculties of memory, reason, and imagination. And they threaded the entries with cross-references directing readers from one article to another. The cross-references did more than assist. A reverent article on an approved doctrine could point the reader toward another, ostensibly unrelated, that treated the same doctrine with irony; an entry on a sacred rite might send the curious to a plain description of similar rites among other peoples.
