The alphabetical order thus concealed an argument conducted in the links, one that censors examining the work entry by entry could not easily detect.

It would be tempting to conclude that alphabetical arrangement is simply liberating because it lets readers assemble their own order. But the reader's freedom is partial. A person who consults an encyclopedia arrives with a question already formed, and the alphabetical format rewards only those questions whose terms the editors anticipated. A reader who does not know that a phenomenon has a name cannot look it up. The thematic encyclopedia, for all its rigidity, can expose a reader to subjects never sought, since browsing a single chapter reveals its neighbors. Each format therefore favors a different kind of curiosity: the alphabetical serves the person who knows what is missing, while the thematic serves the person who does not yet know what to ask.

Digital reference works have revived this debate rather than ended it. Search engines function as an alphabetical index of unprecedented reach, and hyperlinks resemble the Encyclopédie's cross-references, but an unbounded index has no editor to decide what is worth including, and a reader can follow links indefinitely without ever grasping how the subjects fit together. The history suggests that no arrangement is innocent; each embodies a view of what a reader should be able to do with knowledge. The sensible response is not to search for a perfect order but to ask of any arrangement what it makes easy, what it makes hard, and who decided.

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:

options.A: argue that alphabetical arrangement has made encyclopedias more reliable than thematic ones.
options.B: show that the ordering of an encyclopedia reflects assumptions about knowledge and readers, so each arrangement has costs and benefits.
options.C: demonstrate that eighteenth-century editors disguised their real views from the public.
options.D: claim that digital reference works have solved problems of arrangement that print could not.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage traces several arrangements and concludes that none is innocent and each favors something. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not rank reliability and notes costs of alphabetical order. C) The Encyclopédie is one example, not the passage's main point. D) The final paragraph says digital works revived the debate rather than ended it.
questions.trap: Choosing a detailed example (the Encyclopédie) as the main point instead of the passage-wide argument.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a drawback of the alphabetical encyclopedia is that it:

options.A: requires readers to understand the hierarchy of creation before they can locate an entry.
options.B: assigns each topic to a position that depends on the compiler's own theory of the world.
options.C: separates related subjects and depends on readers already knowing the name of what they seek.
options.D: prevents editors from including cross-references between articles on different subjects.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The second and fourth paragraphs say it scatters related topics and rewards only anticipated, named questions. Why the others are wrong: A) That is the drawback of the subject-ordered work. B) Neutrality is the alphabetical order's claimed advantage. D) The Encyclopédie used cross-references within alphabetical order.
questions.trap: Attributing the thematic format's drawback to the alphabetical format by reversing the comparison.

questions.stem: The author mentions the cross-references in the Encyclopédie primarily to illustrate how:

options.A: an apparently neutral arrangement could still carry an argument that readers might miss.
options.B: editors compensated for the fragmentation of knowledge by restoring a cosmic hierarchy.
options.C: censors of the period were generally unable to understand the works they reviewed.
options.D: links between articles are less useful to readers than a tree of knowledge diagram.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The cross-references conducted an argument that entry-by-entry censors could not easily detect. Why the others are wrong: B) The tree diagram, not the links, addressed fragmentation, and it was not a cosmic hierarchy. C) The passage says the links were hard to detect, not that censors lacked understanding. D) No comparison of usefulness is made.
questions.trap: Reading a statement about what was hard to detect as a general claim about the censors' competence.

questions.stem: Which of the following claims about readers is most clearly supported by the fourth paragraph?

options.A: Readers prefer browsing to searching because browsing is faster and more reliable.
options.B: Readers who consult alphabetical works are usually more curious than those who read thematic ones.
options.C: Readers of thematic works may encounter useful subjects that they would not have thought to request.
options.D: Readers of every format ultimately assemble the same order of knowledge for themselves.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Browsing a chapter reveals neighbors, exposing readers to subjects never sought. Why the others are wrong: A) Speed and reliability are not discussed. B) The author says the formats favor different kinds of curiosity, not more or less. D) The author denies that the freedom to assemble one's own order is complete.
questions.trap: Turning a claim of different strengths into a claim that one group is simply better.

questions.stem: Suppose a modern reference site lets users reach any article only by typing its exact title, with no categories or links. Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that this site:

options.A: resembles the medieval encyclopedia because it teaches the order of creation.
options.B: serves readers who know what they are missing but offers little to those who do not know what to ask.
options.C: is the most neutral possible design and therefore free of any assumptions about readers.
options.D: would undermine censorship because it prevents editors from deciding what is included.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Such a site extends the alphabetical logic and rewards only anticipated, named questions. Why the others are wrong: A) The medieval work was ordered by subject, which this site lacks. C) The author says no arrangement is innocent, since each embodies a view of what readers should do. D) Editors still decide what is included; the passage notes only that unbounded indexes lack an editor.
questions.trap: Equating a neutral-looking design with one that makes no assumptions about readers.
